title: e2e latency profiling traces 2026-03-28
content:
Purpose:
Short write-up of end-to-end latency profiling traces captured for the serving-runtime on 2026-03-28. Goal is to surface p50/p95/p99 numbers and per-stage breakdowns, highlight bottlenecks (scheduling, KV-cache, serialization), and propose mitigations. This is a working doc (notes + traces summary); see linked artifacts for raw traces and dashboards.

Summary of findings:
- Baseline workload (steady 600 rps, avg request length 512 tokens, generation length 64 tokens) shows: p50 ~ 130 ms, p95 ~ 380 ms, p99 ~ 820 ms (warm-cache).
- Cold-model or cold-KV-cache traces drive the worst p99s (up to 2.4s) due to disk reads and model weights page-ins on some Dedicated nodes.
- Per-stage breakdown indicates model-inference (kernel execution + scheduling) accounts for ~60-75% of p95/p99; router/queueing + batch-formation contributes ~15-25%; serialization/streaming contributes ~5-10%.

Environment / test config:
- Cluster: dedicated-prod-us-west-2 (8xA100-80GB pools, 64 instance nodes in pool A)
- Serving runtime commit: c3b7f1a (2026-03-26)
- Model tested: open-llm-13B-q4_kv (quantized variant)
- Traffic profile: 600 rps steady for 30 minutes; additional spike tests at 1.2k rps for 10 minutes
- Tracing: OpenTelemetry traces collected at 100% sampling for 30m window, exported to gs://redwood-traces/prod/2026-03-28/
- Measurement window: 2026-03-28 10:00 -> 10:30 UTC

Methodology notes:
- Correlate HTTP request -> routing -> container start -> model inference -> streaming finish spans.
- Spans recorded: ingress-http, auth-check, router-dispatch, queue-wait, batch-formation, kv-cache-lookup, model-inference (kernel), serialization, egress-network.
- Grouped traces by: cache-state (warm/cold), queue depth at arrival, and batch size observed.
- p50/p95/p99 computed over all completed requests in window, and also computed per-group.

Aggregate latency (overall request completion time; ms):
- All requests (warm+cold): p50 = 130 ms, p95 = 380 ms, p99 = 820 ms
- Warm-cache only: p50 = 110 ms, p95 = 310 ms, p99 = 650 ms
- Cold-cache only (first request after model reload or cache miss): p50 = 520 ms, p95 = 1,420 ms, p99 = 2,400 ms
- Spike (1.2k rps): observed p95 jump to ~760 ms and p99 to ~1,900 ms due to increased queueing and larger batch-formation delays.

Per-stage breakdown (warm-cache, median / p95 / p99 in ms):
- ingress-http: p50=3, p95=8, p99=20
- auth-check: p50=1, p95=3, p99=6
- router-dispatch (includes policy routing + route lookup): p50=4, p95=12, p99=30
- queue-wait (time waiting to be batched/scheduled): p50=10, p95=60, p99=220
- batch-formation (time spent assembling batch + copy to GPU): p50=12, p95=45, p99=180
- kv-cache-lookup (prefix/KV cache read + decode): p50=6, p95=20, p99=100
- model-inference (kernel exec + attention op + kv-apply): p50=65, p95=200, p99=430
- serialization/streaming (token framing + chunked responses): p50=7, p95=18, p99=36
- egress-network: p50=8, p95=22, p99=58
- total: p50=130, p95=380, p99=820

Observations on per-stage contributions:
- Model-inference dominates tail (p95/p99). Kernel execution variance correlates with batch-size variance and GPU scheduler preemption events.
- queue-wait and batch-formation are the second-largest tail contributors; these increase significantly under higher QPS and when the autoscaler is concurrently rebalancing pods.
- kv-cache-lookup p99s spike for cold-prefix requests where objects are paged from object-store (S3/remote cache). We see a bimodal distribution: sub-10ms rapid hits vs 200-800ms misses.
- Serialization/egress are relatively stable but account for >10% of p50 in requests with streaming enabled due to small-chunk overhead.

Representative trace examples (warm vs cold):
- Warm trace (typical p95 request): ingress 3ms -> auth 2ms -> router 8ms -> queue 48ms -> batch-formation 40ms -> kv-cache 12ms -> inference 210ms -> serialize 12ms -> egress 10ms = ~345ms total
- Cold trace (p99 cold miss): ingress 4ms -> auth 2ms -> router 10ms -> queue 120ms -> batch-formation 90ms -> kv-cache 680ms (S3 read) -> inference 420ms -> serialize 16ms -> egress 12ms = ~1,354ms total

Hypothesized root causes:
1) Model weight/page-in on some Dedicated nodes causes cold-cache tail (observed disk I/O and >500ms pauses in kv-cache stage). Action: look into pre-warming strategy and VM image locality.
2) Batch-formation variance: large variance caused by opportunistic batching and long tail when single large requests block batch-formation for smaller concurrent requests. Action: enforce max-batch-timeout and per-route batching caps.
3) GPU scheduler preemption / noisy neighbor: some nodes show spikes in model-inference span concurrent with host-level metrics (nv_peer_mem spikes, memory pressure). Action: investigate kube scheduling and pod isolation for critical pools.
4) Remote KV cache misses: objects occasionally not present in local cache leading to S3 reads. Action: increase local cache size or switch to warmer eviction policy for hot prefixes.

Immediate mitigations tested (quick A/B runs):
- Enforced max-batch-timeout = 10ms (was 50ms): reduced queue-wait p95 from 60ms->32ms and p99 from 220->110ms, but increased GPU utilization ~3% and slightly lower throughput.
- Enabled KV-cache prefetch for top-100 prefixes: reduced cold-cache p95 from 1,420ms->620ms for those prefixes.
- Pinned high-traffic routes to a dedicated pool (no autoscaler churn): reduced p95 by ~30% for those routes.

Recommendations / next steps:
1) Short term (1 week):
   - Roll max-batch-timeout = 10ms for high-QPS routes (owner: Carlos Mendes, task: INF-1843).
   - Implement KV-cache prefetch for top prefixes and measure hit-rate improvement (owner: Emily Zhang).
2) Medium term (2-6 weeks):
   - Add model weight pre-warm on node spin-up (daemon that touches pages before accepting traffic). Run A/B to quantify cold-start tail reduction. (owner: Rajiv Menon).
   - Improve batching heuristics: separate large-request lane + small-request lane to reduce blocking. Prototype under feature flag. (owner: Aisha Patel).
3) Long term (quarter):
   - Revisit node isolation and autoscaler policies for Dedicated pools to reduce scheduling-induced variance. Consider GPU reservation for high-priority routes.
   - Consider adding an in-memory local KV-cache tier (e.g., Redis co-located) for extremely hot prefixes to eliminate S3 misses.

Open questions / data to collect:
- Which prefixes account for the majority of cold-cache misses? (need top-N log aggregation).
- Is model weight paging due to kernel-level swapping or container-level lazy loading? Collect vmstat/iostat and container start traces during warmup.
- What is the throughput/latency tradeoff if we reduce max-batch-timeout globally? Need 24h soak.

Notes / low-priority ideas:
- Explore predictive prefetch based on historical prefix access patterns (ML-model).
- Evaluate smaller quantized model variant for tail-sensitive routes to reduce model-inference variance.

Raw assets / where to look:
- Raw traces: gs://redwood-traces/prod/2026-03-28/e2e-traces-100k.jsonl
- Dashboard (p50/p95/p99): https://grafana.internal/redwood/d/serving-runtime/e2e-latency?from=2026-03-28T10:00:00Z&to=2026-03-28T10:30:00Z
- Related PRs / tickets: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/612, Linear INF-1843

Appendix: quick extraction queries used on traces (examples)
- p95 overall: SELECT percentile(duration_ms, 95) FROM traces WHERE span_name = 'request' AND timestamp BETWEEN ...
- per-stage decomposition: aggregate by span_name and compute percentiles grouped by trace_id.

TODOs (owners):

- Emily: build prefetch list for hot prefixes and implement in kv-cache (due 2026-04-07).
- Rajiv: prototype model-weight pre-warm script and run on 3 nodes (due 2026-04-09).
